title: Southern Water's sewer-monitor anomaly model flagged a forming fatberg in Rowner, Gosport, and a crew cleared it before any overflow into the River Alver
summary: Southern Water's AI sewer monitors flagged a forming fatberg in Rowner, Gosport; a crew cleared it before any overflow into the River Alver.
account: Southern Water runs around 34,000 sewer level monitors with machine learning. Its proactive operations control manager Daniel McElhinney says the system learns the normal behavior of sewers. He says it can tell a forming blockage from daily rushes or rain. Shortly before 22 April 2026 the sensors detected an abnormal flow in Rowner, Gosport, and alerted the control room. A crew jetted the sewer and found a fatberg of wet wipes and other unflushable items. The company said that, left unchecked, the sewer could have overflowed from a manhole into a surface water drain leading to the River Alver. The case was reported on 22 April 2026. A second flagged blockage at Warlands Lane, Shalfleet, Isle of Wight, was reported on 23 April.
purpose: The monitors and the anomaly model were installed to spot blockages and leaks forming in sewers. Crews can then clear them before they cause pollution or flooding. This case was that intended use.
system: Southern Water's AI-enabled digital sewer system: a network of around 34,000 sewer level monitors in blockage hotspots with machine learning that learns normal sewer behavior and flags a forming blockage
taxonomy_note: A sewage overflow averted is pollution prevented, which Trustible's description does not name.

ratings.reason: The company says a sewage overflow into the River Alver was averted. The Andover Advertiser says the river is home to herons, water voles and kingfishers. The counterfactual is asserted rather than shown, and no pollution occurred. This is a specific avoided harm of unmeasured size.

Southern Water cleared one blockage before it became a pollution incident or a customer flooding. The company says blocked sewers are the leading cause of its pollution incidents. This is one of the more than 4,000 interventions it reports in a year.

ai_role.statement: The level monitors detected an abnormal flow at Rowner. The machine-learning model raised the alert to the control room; by the company's account it distinguishes a forming blockage from daily rushes and rainfall. The jetting crew found and removed the fatberg. The articles are built on a Southern Water statement and a single quoted manager. They do not name the developer of the model and give no sensor data. No independent party confirmed that an overflow was imminent.

produced_by: Level monitors in sewer blockage hotspots feeding a model that has learned the sewer's normal flow pattern and flags deviations from it
A staffed control room that receives the alert and can dispatch a jetting crew quickly
must_hold: The flagged anomaly is a forming blockage rather than rain or a daily peak, which the company says the model distinguishes but for which no accuracy figures are given
A crew reaches the site before the sewer surcharges; the articles do not say how long that took here
The overflow route the company describes (manhole to surface water drain to river) exists as stated; it is the company's own account

headline: Southern Water's sewer monitors flag a fatberg before overflow

comparator.against: the previous reactive practice of attending blockages after a flooding or pollution event
comparator.before: turning up after the event to clean up and commiserate with devastated customers
comparator.after: spotting hundreds of potential blockages before it is too late
comparator.quote: "Instead of turning up after the event to clean up and commiserate with devastated customers we're spotting hundreds of potential blockages before it's too late."

later.note: The next day the same monitor network flagged a second forming fatberg at Warlands Lane, Shalfleet, on the Isle of Wight, which crews cleared before it reached the Caul Bourne chalk stream.
later.quote: The issue at Warlands Lane, Shalfleet was identified using Southern Water’s network of around 34,000 sewer level monitors, which continuously track flows and detect unusual activity that may indicate a blockage or leak. As the fatberg began to form, sensors alerted the control room, prompting a swift response.
